traveler: Empress Joséphine (Marie-Josèphe-Rose Tascher de La Pagerie, vicomtesse de Beauharnais)
title: The Plantation to the Empty Pedestal: Rose Tascher, the Carmes, and the Crown at Notre-Dame
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Les Trois-Îlets, birth on the Pagerie estate
stops.date_confidence: attested; the birthplace is contested, with a minority Saint Lucian tradition naming Paix Bouche or Babonneau against the mainstream Trois-Îlets reading
stops.campa: On the sugar estate of La Pagerie, in the parish of Les Trois-Îlets across the bay from Fort-Royal, a daughter is born to Joseph-Gaspard Tascher de La Pagerie and Rose-Claire des Vergers de Sannois. They name her Marie-Josèphe-Rose, and the household calls her Rose. The father is a minor noble of Martinique whose fortune is cane, debt, and the enslaved labor of the field. A hurricane has already taken the great house, and the family lives in rooms above the sugar works. Saint Lucia keeps a rival tradition naming Paix Bouche instead; the parish register at Trois-Îlets answers it.
suggested_refs: The Musée de la Pagerie at Les Trois-Îlets, on the ruins of the Tascher sugar works

stops.name: Les Trois-Îlets, baptism at Notre-Dame-de-la-Bonne-Délivrance
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Five weeks after the birth the child is carried to the parish church of Notre-Dame-de-la-Bonne-Délivrance and baptized Marie-Josèphe-Rose. That register is the document by which Martinique holds her against every rival story. She grows up between the cane rows and the sea, in the second rank of the island's white creole gentry, a girl whose family name outranks its money. The legend of Martinique adds a fortune-teller who reads her palm and promises she will be more than a queen. Nobody at the font writes that down.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of the parish of Les Trois-Îlets, 27 July 1763

stops.name: Fort-Royal, the convent school of the Dames de la Providence
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the French sources as the start of the boarding; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At about ten she is sent across the bay to board with the Sisters of Providence in the colonial capital. She learns the accomplishments a planter's daughter is given: music, dancing, embroidery, and enough writing to keep a correspondence. Four years of it. She comes back to the plantation at fourteen with a creole accent that Paris will find charming and an education that Paris will find thin. The estate is failing, and the family begins to look toward France for a marriage that will carry the name where the sugar cannot.
suggested_refs: The convent of the Dames de la Providence at Fort-Royal, Martinique

stops.name: Fort-Royal, embarking on the Île de France
stops.date_confidence: late August 1779 attested; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: Her younger sister Catherine-Désirée, promised to the son of a Beauharnais who had governed the island, died in 1777 before the wedding could happen. The family offers Rose in her place. In the last days of August she goes aboard the flûte Île de France with her father, sixteen years old, betrothed to a man she has never seen. The Atlantic crossing takes months. No source consulted names the port where she came ashore in France. Brest and Nantes are both plausible and neither is attested.
suggested_refs: The flûte Île de France, the vessel of the 1779 crossing

stops.name: Noisy-le-Grand, the marriage to Alexandre de Beauharnais
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the church at Noisy-le-Grand, east of Paris, she marries Alexandre, vicomte de Beauharnais: nineteen years old, an officer, a reader of the philosophes, and a man who will spend the next decade telling her she is provincial. She signs with the hand the nuns taught her. The dowry is modest and partly unpaid. Paris receives the creole bride as an exotic with bad teeth and a good figure, and her husband, ashamed of her, sets about improving her by written syllabus while keeping other company in town.
suggested_refs: The parish church of Noisy-le-Grand, site of the 1779 wedding

stops.name: Paris, the house on the rue Thévenot and two children
stops.date_confidence: the couple's lodging is attested for 1780 and Eugène's birth for 1781; month and day defaulted, as the fetched sources give years only
stops.campa: The couple lodge at the town house of the old marquis de Beauharnais, on the rue Thévenot. Eugène is born in 1781, Hortense in 1783. Alexandre is absent for most of both pregnancies, in Martinique for part of that time, and returns accusing her of infidelity on evidence collected from her own family's enemies on the island. The marriage that produced a future Viceroy of Italy and the mother of a future Emperor of the French lasts, as a household, about four years.
suggested_refs: The hôtel of the marquis de Beauharnais, rue Thévenot, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the abbey of Penthemont
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia dates her entry to 1784 and the court-ordered separation to March 1785; the research pool's 1783 is unsupported and the conflict is left standing
stops.campa: She takes rooms with her children at the abbey of Penthemont on the rue de Grenelle, the house where separated women of quality wait out their lawsuits. The court finds for her. Alexandre is ordered to pay, and she is left with the title, the children, and no money. Penthemont is also a finishing school for the daughters of the aristocracy, and the years there give her what the convent at Fort-Royal did not: the accent and the manners of the world she has married into, and the addresses in it.
suggested_refs: The abbaye de Penthemont, 106 rue de Grenelle, Paris

stops.name: Fontainebleau, three years at the edge of the court
stops.date_confidence: traditional; French Wikipedia dates the stay 1784 to 1787 without a precise arrival, and the pin date is defaulted inside that window
stops.campa: She moves out to Fontainebleau with her aunt Renaudin and the old marquis, living cheaply at the edge of the court's hunting season. Versailles itself stays shut to her: a colonial vicomtesse with a separation decree and no fortune does not get presented. In the same years Adrienne de Noailles, madame de Lafayette, moves through those rooms by right of birth. Rose de Beauharnais will enter the palaces of France only after the Revolution has emptied them of everyone who would have refused her the door.
suggested_refs: The town of Fontainebleau in the hunting seasons of 1784 to 1787

stops.name: Fort-Royal, three years back on the island
stops.date_confidence: June 1788 to November 1790 attested; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: In June 1788 she sails home to Martinique with Hortense, leaving Eugène in France, and stays three years on the family land. The island she returns to is not the island she left. The enslaved population is restive and the free colored population is organizing. News from Paris in 1789 reaches the Antilles as a rumor of general emancipation. In the autumn of 1790 fighting breaks out at Fort-Royal, and she goes down to the harbor with her daughter and takes the first ship out.
suggested_refs: The disturbances at Fort-Royal, Martinique, autumn 1790

stops.name: Toulon, landing from La Sensible
stops.date_confidence: November 1790 attested; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: The frigate La Sensible puts her ashore at Toulon in November: a separated wife with a daughter, no money, and a husband who is now a deputy of the National Assembly and, briefly, its president. Alexandre is a man of the moment, a liberal noble who voted the abolition of privilege. She goes up to Paris and lives on his standing and her aunt's help. For three years the Revolution treats the Beauharnais as its own. Then it changes its mind about people with particles in their names.
suggested_refs: The frigate La Sensible, which carried her back from Martinique in 1790

stops.name: Croissy-sur-Seine, the house of Madame de Hosten
stops.date_confidence: the stay is attested across 1793 to 1794; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: She takes her children out of Paris to the house of her friend Madame de Hosten-Lamotte at Croissy on the Seine, and puts Eugène to a carpenter and Hortense to a seamstress so that the family will show trades and not titles. It is the correct calculation and it fails. Alexandre, who has commanded the Army of the Rhine and lost Mainz, is arrested on 2 March 1794 and taken to the Carmes. By the arithmetic of that spring, the wife of a suspect general is herself a suspect.
suggested_refs: The house of Madame de Hosten-Lamotte at Croissy-sur-Seine

stops.name: Paris, the prison des Carmes
stops.date_confidence: contested: French Wikipedia gives the indictment as 19 April 1794, English Wikipedia gives 21 April, and the research pool's 18 April is supported by neither
stops.campa: The Carmelite convent on the rue de Vaugirard, where the September massacres killed a hundred and fifteen priests in the garden two years earlier, is now a prison, and the stains are still on the walls where guides will later point them out. She is locked into the same house as her husband, alongside Thérésa Cabarrus and the rest of a doomed and famous company. She is thirty. She petitions the Committee to no effect. The prisoners of the Carmes keep the count of who is called out each morning.
suggested_refs: The former Carmelite convent, rue de Vaugirard, prison of the Terror

stops.name: Place de la Révolution, the guillotining of Alexandre
stops.date_confidence: the execution date is attested; the coordinates are the standard modern point for the Place de la Concorde and are a placement of the square, not of the scaffold
stops.campa: Alexandre de Beauharnais goes to the scaffold on the square where Louis XVI died eighteen months before, five days short of the fall of Robespierre that would have saved him. He writes her a last letter calling her his friend. She is still in the Carmes and learns of it there. For those five days the machine on this square keeps taking the names it has been taking, and the widow of a condemned general stands in a queue that is about to be abolished.
suggested_refs: The Place de la Révolution, now the Place de la Concorde, Paris
sources: louis_xvi.journey.json (execution on the same square, 21 January 1793)

stops.name: Paris, released from the Carmes
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia gives 6 August 1794; English Wikipedia's 28 July is not supported by the French text and is flagged rather than resolved
stops.campa: Robespierre falls on 9 Thermidor and is guillotined the next day. She is not freed with him. She comes out nine days after that, on 6 August, through the intervention of Jean-Lambert Tallien and of Thérésa Cabarrus, her fellow prisoner, whom Tallien is about to marry. She leaves the Carmes a widow of thirty-one with two children and a confiscated estate. She also leaves it as a woman who has been inside that building and has come out again, and Paris will pay for that all the next year.
suggested_refs: The Thermidorian releases from the prison des Carmes, August 1794

stops.name: Paris, the house on the rue Chantereine
stops.date_confidence: the Joséphine article implies January 1795, the article on the street dates the lease to late 1795; the street was renamed rue de la Victoire on 28 December 1797 and the house stood at what became nos. 58-60, not no. 50
stops.campa: She takes a small house behind the boulevards, in a street then called Chantereine, and furnishes it on credit. Paris after the Terror is a city of survivors dancing, and she is at the center of it beside Thérésa Tallien, among the women the newspapers call the Merveilleuses. Paul Barras, one of the five directors of the Republic, is her protector and by every account her lover. She has debts, an income made of promises, and an address at which the men who now run France come to dinner.
stops.quote: My waking thoughts are all of thee.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine; Napoleon's Letters to Josephine 1796-1812, ed. and trans. Henry Foljambe Hall (Project Gutenberg ebook 37499), Series A, Letter No. 1, undated, headed 'Seven o'clock in the morning'. Hall's own note dates it 'probably written early in March' 1796.
suggested_refs: The site of nos. 58-60 rue de la Victoire, formerly rue Chantereine, demolished 1858

stops.name: Saint-Germain-en-Laye, the children at school
stops.date_confidence: the schooling is attested for 1795 to 1796; the month is a default inside that window
stops.campa: Eugène boards at the old Irish College and Hortense at the school that Madame Campan, once first chambermaid to Marie-Antoinette, has opened for the daughters of a Republic that beheaded her mistress. The mother drives out from Paris to visit them. Campan's establishment teaches the surviving aristocracy and the new one in the same rooms, and Hortense de Beauharnais, who will be Queen of Holland and the mother of Napoleon III, learns her deportment from a woman who learned it at Versailles.
suggested_refs: Madame Campan's school at Saint-Germain-en-Laye; the Collège des Irlandais

stops.name: Paris, the civil marriage at the mairie of the second municipality
stops.date_confidence: attested; the venue was the Hôtel de Mondragon at 3 rue d'Antin, whose own coordinates (48.8683, 2.3325) sit about three hundred metres from this pin, which is inherited byte-identical from napoleon.journey.json
stops.campa: Past ten at night, in a room of the Hôtel de Mondragon serving as a town hall, she marries General Bonaparte, six years her junior, with Barras among the witnesses. She takes four years off her age on the register and he adds a year and a half to his, so the paper shows two people of twenty-eight. He has already stopped calling her Rose. Two days later he leaves for the Army of Italy without her and begins from the road the flood of letters that will make Joséphine a name in the world.
stops.quote: Every moment separates me further from you, my beloved, and every moment I have less energy to exist so far from you.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, Chanceaux Post House, 14 March 1796; Napoleon's Letters to Josephine 1796-1812, ed. Henry Foljambe Hall (Project Gutenberg ebook 37499), Series A, No. 2. Quoted in full: the shortened form in circulation cuts the closing qualifier without an ellipsis.
suggested_refs: The Hôtel de Mondragon, 3 rue d'Antin, Paris, town hall of the 2nd municipality in 1796

stops.name: Milan, joining the Army of Italy
stops.date_confidence: attested for 9 to 10 July 1796
stops.campa: She has delayed four months, pleading a pregnancy that does not exist, and travels at last in the company of Hippolyte Charles, a hussar lieutenant of twenty-four with a talent for making women laugh. Milan receives her as the wife of the general who broke the Austrians at Lodi and took Lombardy in six weeks. She holds court in the Serbelloni palace. Napoleon comes in from the field for two days at a time, writes to her from the road between, and is told nothing whatever about Charles.
stops.quote: I have beaten the enemy... I am tired to death.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, 6 July 1796; Napoleon's Letters to Josephine 1796-1812, ed. Henry Foljambe Hall (Project Gutenberg ebook 37499)
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Serbelloni, Milan, her residence during the campaign

stops.name: Brescia, following the army east
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The campaign moves and she moves with it, into Brescia at the end of July with a household, a carriage, and an escort. This is the shape of the next year and a half: an army marching, and behind it a small mobile court made of the general's wife, her ladies, her hussar, and the diplomats who have worked out that the shortest road to Bonaparte runs through her. Austrian columns are coming down out of the Tyrol in four separate corps, and nobody in Brescia yet knows where they will fall.
stops.quote: Ceaselessly I recall your kisses, your tears, your enchanting jealousy.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, 17 July 1796; Hall, ed., Napoleon's Letters to Josephine 1796-1812 (Project Gutenberg ebook 37499)
suggested_refs: Brescia in the campaign of the Mincio, July 1796

stops.name: Verona, lodging in the house of Louis XVIII
stops.date_confidence: July 1796 attested; the day is reconstructed from the order of the campaign and should be read as approximate
stops.campa: Wurmser's advance forces her out of Brescia and she is put into Verona, into a house the exiled pretender Louis XVIII had been occupying until the French made the city untenable for him. The Bourbon claimant to the throne of France and the future Empress of the French use the same rooms within months of each other and never meet. Her escort is a squadron of dragoons. The Austrians are a day's march away, and the general writing her love letters cannot spare a regiment to guarantee her road.
stops.quote: My life is a perpetual nightmare. A presentiment of ill oppresses me.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, 15 June 1796; Hall, ed., Napoleon's Letters to Josephine 1796-1812 (Project Gutenberg ebook 37499)
suggested_refs: The Verona lodging of Louis XVIII in exile, vacated in 1796

stops.name: Peschiera del Garda, refusing to leave the fortress
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At the fortress on the outflow of Lake Garda she is told to go and will not go. Wurmser's guns are close enough to be heard from the walls. The account that survives has her weeping in the carriage and refusing the road, and an officer getting her out along the lake shore under fire. She is thirty-three and she has been inside a revolutionary prison; the fear here is real, and by the time the story reaches Paris it is also a piece of theater the regime can use.
stops.quote: I am not satisfied with your last letter; it is cold as friendship.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, 7 April 1796; Hall, ed., Napoleon's Letters to Josephine 1796-1812 (Project Gutenberg ebook 37499)
suggested_refs: The Venetian fortress of Peschiera del Garda, held by the French in July 1796

stops.name: Castelnuovo del Garda, moved on again
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The next day she is at Castelnuovo, south of the lake, one stage further from the fighting. The front is moving faster than her baggage. In these weeks Napoleon will win at Lonato and Castiglione and drive Wurmser back into the mountains, and will complain in writing that she does not answer his letters often enough or warmly enough. She is being carried across northern Italy by an army, and she is bored, and she is writing to Hippolyte Charles. The rumor of it is already moving toward the general's tent.
stops.quote: Away from you there is no more joy; away from thee the world is a wilderness.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, 3 April 1796; Hall, ed., Napoleon's Letters to Josephine 1796-1812 (Project Gutenberg ebook 37499). The Gutenberg text prints an em dash where this transcription uses a semicolon.
suggested_refs: Castelnuovo del Garda, staging point between Peschiera and the Tuscan road

stops.name: Genoa, wintering out of range
stops.date_confidence: November 1796 attested; the day is not recorded. The Lucca stay earlier in 1796 is attested by year only and is folded into this stop
stops.campa: She is sent to Lucca in the summer and to Genoa in November, out of reach of the Austrian columns, and receives the republics of Italy as though she were already what she will be in eight years. In the same month Napoleon crosses the marshes at Arcole and comes close to dying there. He writes to her afterward like a man coming up out of water. The letters of this autumn are the most extreme he will ever write to anyone, and she answers them, when she answers, in the register of a friend.
stops.quote: Once more I breathe freely. Death is no longer before me.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, 19 November 1796, after Arcole; Hall, ed., Napoleon's Letters to Josephine 1796-1812 (Project Gutenberg ebook 37499)
suggested_refs: The Ligurian Republic at Genoa, 1796; the marshes of Arcole

stops.name: Mombello, the court in the villa
stops.date_confidence: the villa occupancy is attested from 16 May to 18 November 1797; the coordinates correct the research pool's point, which fell nine to ten kilometres away
stops.campa: At the Villa Crivelli Pusterla at Mombello, north of Milan, the general keeps something that is not yet a court and is no longer a headquarters. Ambassadors are received in audience. His mother and his sisters arrive from Corsica, and Elisa and Paolina are married in the chapel on 14 June. The Bonaparte women look at Joséphine and decide against her, permanently. She presides over dinners of thirty. In October the Treaty of Campo Formio ends the war, and the household that has followed an army for a year goes home.
suggested_refs: The Villa Crivelli Pusterla at Mombello, frazione of Limbiate, Napoleon's headquarters May to November 1797

stops.name: Toulon, the fleet sails for Egypt
stops.date_confidence: May 1798 attested; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: She travels down to Toulon with him in May as the Egyptian expedition loads: four hundred ships, thirty-eight thousand men, and a shipload of scholars. She is to follow on a later vessel and she never does. The plan is abandoned, and no source consulted explains why. She goes instead to take the waters. Within months her husband, in Cairo, will be told about Hippolyte Charles by his own officers, and will write to his brother that the veil has been torn.
suggested_refs: The embarkation of the Armée d'Orient at Toulon, May 1798

stops.name: Rueil-Malmaison, the purchase of the château
stops.date_confidence: attested for 21 April 1799
stops.campa: With her husband on the Nile and unreachable for months at a time, she buys the estate of Malmaison on the Seine west of Paris for three hundred and twenty-five thousand francs, most of it borrowed. The house is dilapidated and the park runs to two hundred and sixty hectares. It is the largest decision she ever takes alone and the one that outlives everything else she owns. He is furious about the price when he returns, and then he is at Malmaison every week, and then the Consulate is half governed from its rooms.
suggested_refs: The Château de Malmaison, bought 21 April 1799 for 325,000 francs

stops.name: Plombières-les-Bains, the fall from the balcony
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Taking the cure in the Vosges, she is standing on a wooden balcony with five other women when it gives way and drops the party into the street. She is badly hurt and immobile for weeks. The waters at Plombières are prescribed for barrenness, which is what she has come for and what she will not get. The accident enters the national repertory afterward as an omen. At the time it is a broken balcony in a spa town, and it keeps her out of Paris in the summer before Brumaire.
suggested_refs: The thermal baths of Plombières-les-Bains and the balcony collapse of 20 June 1799

stops.name: Paris, installed in the Tuileries
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinates inherited byte-identical from napoleon.journey.json
stops.campa: Four months after Brumaire the First Consul moves into the palace of the kings, and she moves in with him, into the ground-floor apartments that had been Marie-Antoinette's. She is said to have wept on the first night. The court of France is being rebuilt around a Corsican artillery officer and a creole widow, and it is her business rather than his to teach the new Republic's generals and their wives how to come into a room. She is good at it, and it is the qualification the regime actually needs.
suggested_refs: The ground-floor apartments of the Tuileries, occupied from 19 February 1800

stops.name: Paris, the bomb in the rue Saint-Nicaise
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve the party leaves the Tuileries for the opera in two carriages. A cart with a powder barrel is standing in the rue Saint-Nicaise. The First Consul's carriage is through before it goes off; hers, delayed because a shawl was being arranged, is close enough that the glass comes in and Hortense is cut. Twenty-two people in the street are killed. Napoleon goes on to the opera and sits through the performance. The plot is royalist, and the Consulate deports a hundred and thirty Jacobins for it anyway.
suggested_refs: The machine infernale of the rue Saint-Nicaise, 24 December 1800

stops.name: Rueil-Malmaison, the roses and Redouté
stops.date_confidence: the collection of nearly two hundred new varieties is attested for 1803; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: She is growing close to two hundred plants new to France, in a heated orangery built to hold three hundred pineapples and in glasshouses supplied by Kew and by the botanists of the Cape through a wartime blockade her husband's navy is enforcing. The Admiralty in London issues passes for her seeds. Pierre-Joseph Redouté paints what comes up. His roses, printed after her death, are the reason the name survives in a nursery catalogue as well as in a dynasty.
suggested_refs: Pierre-Joseph Redouté, Les Roses, painted from the Malmaison collection

stops.name: Cologne, the imperial progress on the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinates inherited byte-identical from salomon_oppenheim.journey.json
stops.campa: Two months before the coronation, the Emperor and Empress enter Cologne through the Eigelstein gate on a progress through the annexed left bank: triumphal arches, illuminations, silver medals struck for diligent schoolchildren. Watching from the merchant city is the house of Oppenheim, whose founder Salomon Oppenheim has been made a citizen and a notable banker by the Code that carries the visiting Emperor's name. The couple travel now as a single institution. The Senate proclaimed him Emperor in May, and the title she carries is his.
suggested_refs: Napoleon's entry into Cologne, 13 September 1804, contemporary prints

stops.name: Paris, crowned in Notre-Dame
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinates inherited byte-identical from napoleon.journey.json
stops.campa: The night before, at her insistence, Cardinal Fesch marries them in a religious ceremony the Pope has demanded and Napoleon has avoided for eight years. It is the sacrament that will make the annulment difficult later. In the cathedral the next day he crowns himself and then turns and sets the smaller crown on her head as she kneels. David paints that second gesture rather than the first. Pope Pius VII attends and does not officiate. She is forty-one, the widow of a guillotined vicomte, and Empress of the French.
suggested_refs: Jacques-Louis David, Le Sacre de Napoléon, 1807, Louvre

stops.name: Milan, the Iron Crown in the Duomo
stops.date_confidence: the coronation of 26 May 1805 is attested and corrects the research pool's 23 May; her own presence at the ceremony is stated in general accounts but is not confirmed in the sources consulted, and she was not herself crowned. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from napoleon.journey.json
stops.campa: He crowns himself a second time in the Duomo, with the Iron Crown of the Lombards. She holds the consort title of Queen of Italy and is not herself crowned, and the French account of the ceremony does not place her in the building. Nine years earlier she came into this city behind an army, a general's wife with a hussar in her carriage. The court she keeps now is the one she invented at Mombello, enlarged to the size of a kingdom and staffed with people who owe her their places.
suggested_refs: The Iron Crown of Lombardy, Monza; the Milan coronation of 26 May 1805

stops.name: Paris, the divorce read out in the Tuileries
stops.date_confidence: the civil divorce is signed 15 December 1809 and registered by senatus-consulte on 16 December; the ecclesiastical annulment follows in January 1810, and the research pool's single date of 10 January 1810 conflated the two
stops.campa: He told her on 30 November, at dinner, with the servants sent out of the room. On 15 December, in the small salon before the assembled family, the act is read: fourteen years dissolved for reasons of state, and she cannot finish reading her own consent aloud. The Senate registers it the next day. In January the diocesan court of Paris annuls the religious marriage of 1804 on a technicality about a missing parish priest. She keeps the title of Empress, she keeps Malmaison, and the letters keep coming.
suggested_refs: The senatus-consulte of 16 December 1809; the annulment by the Officialité de Paris, January 1810

stops.name: Évreux, Duchess of Navarre
stops.date_confidence: April 1810 attested for the grant; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: He makes her Duchess of Navarre and gives her a cold, damp, badly built château near Évreux, a pension of five million francs a year, and the understanding that she will be out of Paris while the Austrian archduchess arrives. Marie Louise is married to him at Compiègne on 2 April. Joséphine spends the spring in Normandy replanting a park she does not like, reads her stepson's letters, and negotiates by post for permission to come back to Malmaison, which is hers outright and always was.
suggested_refs: The Château de Navarre near Évreux, demolished in the nineteenth century

stops.name: Rueil-Malmaison, the news of the King of Rome
stops.date_confidence: the birth of Napoleon II on 20 March 1811 is attested and corrects the research pool's 11 March; her counting of the guns at Malmaison is the traditional account
stops.campa: The cannon of Paris fire a hundred and one times on 20 March, and she counts them from Malmaison. Marie Louise has produced the heir, styled King of Rome, that thirteen years of her own marriage did not. She writes to congratulate him and he answers. By dynastic arithmetic her own children have done better than she has: Eugène is Viceroy of Italy, Hortense is Queen of Holland, and Hortense's third son will be Emperor of the French in forty-one years, which no cannon announces today.
suggested_refs: The hundred and one guns for the King of Rome, Paris, 20 March 1811

stops.name: Rueil-Malmaison, the Tsar in the garden
stops.date_confidence: the visits are attested for spring 1814 and the pool gives May 1814; the specific days are not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Napoleon has abdicated and gone to Elba, and the allied sovereigns are in Paris. Alexander I of Russia comes out to Malmaison, and so do the King of Prussia and half the occupying command, to call on the divorced Empress in her rose garden. She receives them in light dresses in a cold spring. She is protecting her children's position: Eugène's title and Hortense's pension are being settled in these rooms and on these gravel walks, by a woman with no legal standing at all.

stops.name: Rueil-Malmaison, death at Malmaison
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinates follow Wikipedia's 48.87083 N, 2.16694 E and correct the research pool's afterlife point, which lay 1.6 km northeast
stops.campa: She dies of pneumonia on the morning of 29 May, fifty years old, in the house she bought with borrowed money while her husband was in Egypt. Hortense and Eugène are with her. The tradition holds that the chill came from walking in the garden with the Tsar in a thin gown. Twenty thousand people file past the body. On Elba, Napoleon shuts himself in his room for two days when the newspapers reach him. The gardens go on flowering through the occupation.
stops.quote: I truly loved my Joséphine, but I did not respect her.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Napoleon at Saint Helena; cited at the Wikipedia article 'Joséphine de Beauharnais', footnote 31, and probably deriving from Las Cases, Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène. The primary text was not consulted and the attribution is unverified.

sources: English and French Wikipedia, 'Joséphine de Beauharnais'

stops.name: Rueil-Malmaison, buried in Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul
stops.date_confidence: June 1814 attested; the day is not fixed in the sources consulted and is defaulted. The coordinates follow the French article on the church, 48 52 35 N 2 10 53 E, against two other values in the research pool
stops.campa: She is carried down to the parish church of Rueil and buried there, a mile and a half from her own front door, with the Beauharnais children and the crowd of the town walking behind. There is no imperial funeral. The Empire has fallen and the Bourbons are back in the Tuileries. Her debts at death run to about three million francs and Hortense will pay them. The body will wait in the cellar of the presbytery for eleven years while the monument is carved.

segments.name: The Tomb, the House, and the Statue

stops.name: Rueil-Malmaison, the tomb completed
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eleven years after the burial the marble is finished and she is installed in it: Pierre Cartellier's Carrara figure, kneeling, hands together, in the coronation dress. The architect is Louis-Martin Berthault, who laid out her gardens at Malmaison. The pose is copied from David's canvas, so the tomb shows not the woman but the painting of the woman, at the exact instant she was crowned. Hortense will lie in the crypt from 1856, with a cenotaph by Barre facing her mother across the nave.

stops.name: Fort-de-France, the statue in La Savane
stops.date_confidence: the installation is attested for 1859; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Her grandson, now Napoleon III, sets a marble Joséphine in the public garden of La Savane at Fort-de-France, facing across the bay toward Trois-Îlets where she was born. Martinique is given an empress of its own, in coronation robes, holding a medallion of her husband. The island is eleven years past emancipation. In 1802 the Consulate had reimposed slavery in the French colonies, and the planter families of Martinique had reason to be grateful for a creole in the Tuileries.
suggested_refs: The marble Joséphine of La Savane, Fort-de-France, erected 1859

stops.name: Rueil-Malmaison, the château becomes a museum
stops.date_confidence: the museum opening is attested for 1905 and the bequest for 1904; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Eugène inherited the house. His widow sold it in 1828; a Swedish banker had it, then the Queen Mother of Spain, then Napoleon III, then the Prussians, who ransacked the interior in 1870 and quartered soldiers in the rooms. The park went to builders in 1877. In 1896 Daniel Iffla, called Osiris, bought what was left, restored it with the architect Pierre Humbert, and gave it to France with his Napoleonic collection in 1904. It opens as a national museum in 1905, ninety-one years after she died upstairs.
suggested_refs: The Musée national des châteaux de Malmaison et Bois-Préau, opened 1905

stops.name: Fort-de-France, the statue beheaded
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1991; the month is not recorded in the source consulted, and the repainting recurs in most years afterward
stops.campa: The statue in La Savane is decapitated in the night and its neck and shoulders painted red. The city does not repair it. Every few years the paint is renewed. Martinican opinion has fixed on the law of 20 May 1802 restoring slavery in the colonies, and on a local tradition, unproven in any document reached, that the creole Empress asked her husband for it. The headless marble stands in the middle of the capital for thirty years, and the guidebooks explain it to visitors.
suggested_refs: The 1802 law restoring slavery in the French colonies; the 1991 decapitation in La Savane

stops.name: Fort-de-France, the empty pedestal
stops.date_confidence: July 2020 attested; the day is not recorded, and no replacement monument is confirmed in any source consulted
stops.campa: In the weeks after George Floyd is killed in Minneapolis, activists pull the headless statue off its base and break it. What is left in La Savane is a pedestal. Claude Lévi-Strauss, interned in this town in 1941 on his way out of occupied Europe, walked past the figure when it still had a head. No source checked confirms that a replacement has been installed. Two hundred and fifty-seven years after Trois-Îlets, the island keeps the plinth and declines the empress.
